section.title: The Prophetic Word Confirmed
section.sectionRationale: Knowing his death is near, Peter explains why he keeps reminding the church of these truths, then anchors them in two unshakable witnesses: what he saw with his own eyes at the Transfiguration, and the prophetic word of Scripture, which came not from human will but from the Holy Spirit.
section.thesis: The gospel is no cleverly devised fable; Peter was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, shine as a reliable lamp until Christ the morning star dawns.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Peter's farewell reminder, verses 12 to 15; the eyewitness of Christ's majesty, verses 16 to 18; and the prophetic word and its divine origin, verses 19 to 21.

verses.text: Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have.
I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the {{skenoma|tent of my body}},
because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me.
And I will make every effort to ensure that after my {{exodos|departure}}, you will be able to recall these things at all times.

For we did not follow {{mythos|cleverly devised fables}} when we made known to you the power and {{parousia|coming}} of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were {{epoptes|eyewitnesses}} of His {{megaleiotes|majesty}}.
For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.

We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the {{phosphoros|morning star}} rises in your hearts.
Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from {{epilysis|one’s own interpretation}}.
For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were {{pheromenoi|carried along}} by the Holy Spirit.

skenoma.gloss: A tent, dwelling, or lodging, used here for the body. Peter speaks of living in the tent of his body, a temporary shelter soon to be taken down. The image conveys that the body is a passing dwelling, while the person continues beyond death.

exodos.gloss: A departure, exit, or going out; the word behind Exodus. Peter calls his coming death his departure. The same word is used of Jesus at the Transfiguration in Luke 9:31, framing death for the believer as a purposeful going out, not mere extinction.

mythos.gloss: A myth, fable, or invented tale. Peter insists the apostles did not follow cleverly devised myths when they proclaimed Christ. The gospel is grounded in witnessed events, not in the fictions the false teachers would later spin.

parousia.gloss: A coming, arrival, or presence, the standard term for Christ's second coming. Peter proclaims the power and parousia of the Lord Jesus. The Transfiguration was a preview of the glory in which He will return.

epoptes.gloss: An eyewitness, one who has seen with his own eyes. Peter, James, and John were epoptai of Christ's majesty on the mountain. Their testimony rests on firsthand sight, not secondhand report, making the gospel a matter of history.

megaleiotes.gloss: Majesty, magnificence, greatness. At the Transfiguration the apostles beheld the megaleiotes of Christ, His divine glory shining through. It confirmed that Jesus is the beloved Son, honored and glorified by the Father.

phosphoros.gloss: The light-bringer, the morning star that heralds the dawn. Peter longs for this star to rise in his readers' hearts. It points to Christ Himself, whose full appearing will end the night and complete what the prophetic lamp now guides us through.

epilysis.gloss: A loosing, unraveling, or interpretation. Peter says no prophecy of Scripture came from one's own epilysis. Whether this means the prophet's own origination or the reader's private interpretation, the point is that Scripture's source is God, not human invention.

pheromenoi.gloss: Being carried, borne, or driven along, as a ship is carried by the wind. The prophets spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. God moved them so that their words are truly His, even as they remained active human authors.

basic.context: Peter knows he will die soon, so he explains why he keeps repeating these truths: he wants the church to remember them after he is gone. Then he gives two solid reasons to trust the gospel. First, he saw Jesus glorified with his own eyes on the mountain and heard God's voice call Him beloved Son. The message is not a made-up story. Second, the Scriptures of the prophets are even more sure, a lamp for a dark world, because they did not come from human imagination but from men moved by the Holy Spirit.
basic.hermeneutics: The great subject here is where Scripture comes from. Verses 20 to 21 teach that prophecy did not originate in the prophet's own mind or will; the prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit, so their words are God's words. This is a foundational text for the inspiration of Scripture. Peter also links his eyewitness experience to the written word, and then says the written word is even more confirmed, so we test experience by Scripture, not the other way round.
basic.originalLanguages: Peter lives in the skenoma, the tent, of his body and awaits his exodos, his departure, like Jesus at the Transfiguration. The gospel is no mythos, no fable, for the apostles were epoptai, eyewitnesses, of Christ's megaleiotes, majesty, and His coming parousia. So we heed the prophetic lamp until the phosphoros, the morning star, rises. Scripture came from no human epilysis, for the prophets were pheromenoi, carried along, by the Holy Spirit.
basic.typology: The Transfiguration is a preview of Christ's second coming in glory, a mountain-top glimpse of the majesty in which He will return. Peter calling his death an exodos echoes the exodus from Egypt and Jesus' own departure, framing the believer's death as a passage to glory. And the morning star fulfills the ancient hope of a rising light, realized in Christ.
basic.christ: Christ is the majesty the apostles beheld, the beloved Son honored by the Father's voice, and the coming King whose glory the Transfiguration foreshadowed. He is the morning star whose dawning the whole prophetic word anticipates. Every line points to Him: seen in glory, declared by God, promised by the prophets, and awaited in His return.
basic.god: God the Father speaks from heaven, honoring His Son, and God the Holy Spirit carries the prophets so their words are truly divine. Here the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are all at work. God is the ultimate author of Scripture, the one whose voice validated Christ and whose Spirit inspired the prophets.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 17:1-8 records the Transfiguration Peter witnessed. Second Timothy 3:16 says all Scripture is God-breathed. Luke 9:31 calls Jesus' coming death His exodus, the word Peter uses. And Revelation 22:16 names Jesus the bright morning star.
basic.oneStory: God spoke through the prophets, carried by His Spirit, and then in the fullness of time revealed His Son in majesty, witnessed by Peter on the mountain. The written word and the seen glory agree, both pointing to Christ, the morning star whose full dawning the church awaits. Scripture is the reliable lamp lighting the whole story until He appears.

context.literary:
The passage is the close of the letter's opening movement and it works as a hinge. Verses 3 to 11 laid out the ladder of virtues and the call to make one's calling sure. Verses 12 to 15 now say why Peter is writing at all, and verses 16 to 21 supply the ground on which the whole letter will stand, a double witness, one heard on a mountain and one written in the prophets. Chapter 2 will then turn to teachers who tamper with exactly this foundation, and chapter 3 will return to the same two witnesses, the prophets and the apostles, in 3:2.

The argument is built in matched pairs. Peter will remind (verse 12) so that they can recall (verse 15). The apostles were not following invented stories (verse 16) but did see and hear (verses 16 to 18). The first witness is what the apostles heard, 'we ourselves heard this voice', and the second is what the prophets wrote, so that eye and ear are set beside a text. The little word 'we' carries the first half; the command 'you will do well to pay attention' carries the second.

There is also a movement from the past to the future inside the single paragraph. Verse 18 sits on a mountain years earlier. Verse 19 speaks of a lamp for the present dark. Verse 19 ends with a day that has not yet dawned. The reader is walked from memory to obedience to hope in six verses.

Verses 20 and 21 are sentence pairs built on a negative and a positive: not from one's own unravelling, not by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along. The 'above all' of verse 20 (the same phrase opens 3:3) marks these as the first things a reader must grasp. Peter is writing a testament, and a testament puts the weightiest matter last and says it twice.
context.historical:
Second Peter belongs to the final stretch of Peter's life. Jesus had told him in John 21:18 and 19 that he would be taken where he did not want to go, and Peter now says the Lord has made the nearness of his death clear to him, verse 14. Early Christian tradition places his death in Rome in the time of Nero, in the 60s, though the letter itself gives neither place nor date. What the letter does give is the tone of a man preparing to leave, and the Greek word for departure he uses, exodos, is the same word Luke gives to the subject of Moses' and Elijah's talk with Jesus on the mountain, Luke 9:31.

The readers are churches in a world full of competing religious stories. Pagan religion offered the myths of gods who took human shape, mystery cults offered secret visions, and Greek philosophers like the Epicureans mocked any idea of divine intervention or a final judgment. Into that setting, to say that the gospel was a set of invented tales was an easy charge to make. Peter's answer is to point to a date, a place and named witnesses. The holy mountain is the Transfiguration, which the Gospels place about a week after Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, Matthew 16:13 to 17:1, and which Peter, James and John alone attended, Matthew 17:1.

To a Jewish ear the scene echoes Sinai. Moses went up the mountain on the seventh day, the glory of the LORD settled as a cloud, and the sight was like a consuming fire, Exodus 24:15 to 18. A bright cloud, a voice, shelters (Peter's offer to build three, Matthew 17:4, recalls the tent of meeting and the Feast of Booths) and Moses himself standing beside Jesus would all have said to a first century Jew that the God of Sinai was present again.

The prophets whom Peter appeals to are not only the writing prophets. For a Jew, the Law, the Prophets and the Writings were all the voice of the Spirit, and David could say, 'The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue,' 2 Samuel 23:2. That is the settled belief Peter relies on.
context.canonical:
The Transfiguration is told in all three Synoptic Gospels, Matthew 17:1 to 8, Mark 9:2 to 8 and Luke 9:28 to 36, and Peter's account differs in telling ways. He omits the command 'Listen to Him', which Matthew 17:5 and Luke 9:35 record, and the omission is probably because his whole letter is an extended 'listen to Him' by another route. Only Luke records that Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' 'departure', Luke 9:31, the word Peter takes up for himself in verse 15. John does not narrate the scene, yet his opening testimony, 'We have seen His glory', John 1:14, is the same claim of eyewitness.

The voice from heaven weaves three Old Testament texts together: the royal Son of Psalm 2:7, the chosen Servant of Isaiah 42:1, and the beloved son of Abraham, Genesis 22:2. In the Gospels it also leads straight to Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. The Father's voice at the mountain and at the Jordan, Matthew 3:17, therefore frames Jesus' ministry as the arrival of everything the Law and Prophets pointed to.

What Peter says about Scripture is echoed throughout the canon. Paul writes that 'All Scripture is God-breathed', 2 Timothy 3:16, which names the source (God's breath) where Peter names the means (the Spirit carrying the writers). Peter himself says in 1 Peter 1:10 to 12 that the prophets searched carefully into the very salvation they wrote of, and that the Spirit of Christ was in them. Hebrews 1:1 to 2 draws the same line from the prophets to the Son. In the last pages of Scripture the 'morning star' returns twice, once as a gift promised to the overcomer, Revelation 2:28, and once as a name of Jesus Himself, Revelation 22:16, so that Peter's closing image comes round again at the end of the Bible.

Peter will pair this verdict with a remarkable statement about Paul, in 3:15 and 16, treating his letters as 'Scriptures'. The canon is already forming under his hand.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wants the churches to be able to say, long after his death, why they believe what they believe. His method is deliberate. He does not ask them to trust his authority alone, and he does not ask them to trust a private religious experience. He offers two things that can be checked against each other: a public event with named witnesses, and a body of writing already in their hands.

The repeated 'always' and 'at all times' of verses 12 and 15 show that Peter expects the danger to come after he is gone, and that he is deliberately leaving behind a means of resisting it. The reminder will outlast him because the letter itself is the reminder. The writing of verse 15 ('I will make every effort to ensure') is itself the effort.

The point of verses 20 and 21 is protective. Peter is about to describe teachers who will twist Scripture, and he first fixes where Scripture comes from. If the prophets spoke from their own heads, any teacher's head would do as well. Because they spoke from God, the Scriptures stand over every teacher, including the one who is writing. Peter intends his readers to hold the text with reverence, to attend to it like a lamp in the dark, and to keep watching for the dawn.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 16 to 18 describe what happened on one mountain to three men; they do not promise that every believer will see such glory. Peter does not tell the churches to seek a vision. He says that one real vision stands behind the message already given. Readers who read the passage as a pattern for chasing spiritual experience have turned a witness into a method.

The prescription is in verse 19: 'you will do well to pay attention.' That command is for every generation, and it is an instruction to pay attention to a lamp, not to the fire of a bonfire. Notice also that Peter does not diminish the apostles' experience when he calls the prophetic word 'more' sure; he says the written word is the lasting means by which the church holds what the apostles saw.

Verses 20 and 21 describe the origin of Scripture. They are not a recipe for interpretation, and they do not forbid ordinary people to read the Bible for themselves. Elsewhere Peter treats believers as a priesthood who can read, 1 Peter 2:9, and Acts 17:11 commends those who examined the Scriptures daily.

debates.question: What does 'one's own interpretation' mean in verse 20?

views.label: Prophets did not originate their own message
views.case: Verse 21 begins with 'For' and explains verse 20: the reason no prophecy is of private unloosing is that none was brought forth by human will. On this reading the issue is where the prophecy came from. The prophets did not decode events and then announce their private conclusions; God gave the message. This is the reading favored by most commentators, since it matches the sentence structure and the surrounding talk of origin.

views.label: Readers must not interpret Scripture privately
views.case: A long tradition, especially in Roman Catholic teaching, reads the verse as a rule for the reader: Scripture is not to be interpreted by individual judgment apart from the church. The Reformers answered that the context is about the prophets' source, and that the Bible is plain enough for the faithful to read.

views.label: Both, in a limited sense
views.case: Some say the verse is about origin first, but that its logic carries over: if Scripture came from God's Spirit, it should be read in dependence on the same Spirit and within the people He formed, not as a private puzzle. This protects the doctrine of inspiration while still warning against the lone, self-confident reader.

debates.bearing: The flow of the argument favors the first view, because verse 21 is the explanation, but the warning about private cleverness is not wasted: 3:16 shows that distortion was a live danger. A reader who humbly asks what the text meant, and tests it against the rest of Scripture, honors both.

debates.question: What is the prophetic word 'more' confirmed, verse 19?

views.label: More sure than the Transfiguration
views.case: The comparative can be read as a ranking: the written prophets are a firmer ground than even the apostles' experience, because Scripture is permanent and open to all, while the mountain was seen by three. This fits the stress on 'pay attention'.

views.label: Made more sure by the Transfiguration
views.case: Others take the comparative as an effect: the mountain has strengthened the prophets' word, since the glory seen there is what they foretold. On this reading, the apostles' sight does not outrank the prophets but confirms them, and Peter's 'we also have' links the two.

views.label: Equal witnesses, each confirming the other
views.case: A few see no ranking at all, only two witnesses that agree. Peter wants the readers to see that the apostles' testimony and the prophets' words lock together.

debates.bearing: The ranking views make better sense of verse 20, which turns at once to Scripture's origin. In every reading the lesson holds that experience is to be tested by the written word, and that the written word is vindicated, not replaced, by what the apostles saw.

debates.question: When does the morning star rise 'in your hearts'?

views.label: At Christ's return
views.case: The lamp lasts 'until the day dawns', and Peter's letter is oriented toward the Day of the Lord in chapter 3. The dawn is the public arrival of Christ, when the lamp of prophecy will no longer be needed.

views.label: In inner illumination now
views.case: The words 'in your hearts' suggest something happening inside the believer. On this reading, the dawn is the moment the prophetic word becomes light in a person's heart, as in 2 Corinthians 4:6.

views.label: The inner and the future together
views.case: Many join the two: the final dawn is Christ's appearing, and its beginnings are already felt in the heart of the believer who trusts the word, the pattern of the 'already and not yet'.

debates.bearing: 'Until' ties the image to a limit in time, so the final coming is surely in view, but the reference to the heart reminds us that waiting is not idle; the believer already walks by a light that comes from the day it awaits.

study.originalLanguages:
Peter's Greek choices show how carefully he is arguing. In verse 16 the 'cleverly devised' stories translates a perfect participle of sophizo, from the same root as sophos, wise: they were stories made clever, crafted. Peter's denial is that the gospel is a product of human ingenuity. The word is used again by Peter in this letter only here, and the cluster 'we did not follow' reminds a reader that the teachers of chapter 2 will be the ones following their own devices.

The verb in verse 17, to be 'well pleased', is eudokeo, a word the Gospels use at the Jordan and on the mountain, Matthew 3:17 and 17:5, and which Matthew 12:18 uses when he quotes Isaiah 42:1 of God's chosen Servant. The Father's delight is taken from the Servant Songs, and it is spoken here of a Son.

In verse 19 'confirmed beyond doubt' is built on bebaios, a word for what is firm, stable, reliable. The word is used of a promise that is guaranteed in Romans 4:16 and of the message that proved reliable in Hebrews 2:2 and 3. It is a comparative form, 'more sure', and the sense of the comparison is exactly what the debate above turns on. Peter calls the prophetic word, in a phrase, the prophetic logos: the whole body of Scripture under a single heading.

The image of the lamp uses lychnos, the ordinary oil lamp of a house, the kind Psalm 119:105 had in mind when it called God's word 'a lamp to my feet'. The 'dark place' is the same world that 2:17 will call a place of blackest darkness for the false teachers, and the contrast between the lamp and the dawn is a contrast between an interim light and a final one. The verb for 'dawns' is a compound, diaugazo, meaning to shine through, and it is only used here in the New Testament, so the light is pictured as breaking through the gloom.

What Peter says of the prophets in verse 21 is carefully worded. Prophecy was never 'brought forth', a form of the verb phero, by human will, yet the prophets did speak, and they spoke 'from God' while being 'carried along', another form of the same verb. The repetition is deliberate: the text was carried to men, and men were carried by the Spirit. The same verb in Acts 27:15 and 17 is used of a ship driven by the wind, so that the image is of a sail filled by a breath that is not the sailor's own, with the sailor still at the helm. That balance guards against two errors: the idea that the prophets were mere machines, and the idea that they were authors in their own right.

Finally, Peter's pair of verbs for his reminding work, hypomimnesko and, in verse 15, spoudazo, 'make every effort', show a man who treats memory as a labor. The same verb for effort returns in 1:10 and again in 3:14, tying the reminder to the whole shape of the letter.

typology.type: The Transfiguration and the glory at Sinai, verses 16 to 18
typology.fulfillment: On Sinai the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain in cloud and fire and Moses went up into it, Exodus 24:15 to 18. On the holy mountain the glory was no longer that of a distant fire but of a Man, whose face 'shone like the sun', Matthew 17:2. Moses, who had seen the glory from the cloud, now stands beside the One whose glory it was. The escalation is that the Law-giver and the greatest prophet step aside and the Father's voice says to listen to the Son, Matthew 17:5. The correspondence falls short as a pattern for believers: Moses' face reflected glory and faded, 2 Corinthians 3:7 and 13, while the glory on Jesus is His own and lasting.

typology.type: Peter's exodos and the exodus, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: In Luke 9:31 Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus about His 'departure', exodos, which He is to accomplish at Jerusalem, and Peter uses the same word for his own death. The shape of the exodus, a people brought out of bondage by a mighty act, becomes the shape of Jesus' death and resurrection, and Peter, who follows Him, sees his own end as a smaller exodus walking behind the first. The escalation is that Christ's departure is the deliverance, while Peter's departure is only the passage of one delivered. The pattern is not exact: Jesus' exodos is accomplished for others, 1 Peter 2:24, and Peter's is not.

typology.type: The lamp and the morning star, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: The lamp in the tabernacle, tended night after night, Exodus 27:20 and 21, and the lamp of God's word in Psalm 119:105 both give light in the dark until morning. Balaam's oracle looks for a star coming forth from Jacob, Numbers 24:17, and Jesus names Himself 'the bright Morning Star', Revelation 22:16. The escalation is from a light that serves the night to the light that ends it; the lamp points to what the sun will make plain. The type falls short in that a lamp can be put out or left unlit, while the Star rises by His own power.

typology.type: The three shelters and the tent of the body, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Peter's offer to build three shelters, Matthew 17:4, reaches back toward the tabernacle and the Feast of Booths, where Israel lived in huts to remember God's dwelling with them. In the letter Peter himself lives in a tent, and his body is a temporary dwelling soon to be laid aside, as Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:1. The fulfillment comes when God makes His dwelling with man in the new creation, Revelation 21:3, and the tent gives way to a permanent home. The type falls short because both tabernacle and body are provisional, while the dwelling to come has no end.

study.christ:
Peter's whole defence of the faith rests on the glory of a particular person, and the Gospels explain why that glory could be seen at all. In John 1:14 the Word 'made His dwelling among us', the very picture of a tent pitched among men, and the glory on the mountain was the glory that had been veiled in the manger. Peter was permitted to see through the veil for a moment. The word majesty in verse 16 belongs to the vocabulary of divine greatness, and Peter ascribes it to Jesus without any hint of strain.

The Father's voice shows the Son from three directions. He is King, as in Psalm 2:7. He is the Servant on whom the Spirit rests, as in Isaiah 42:1, and so He suffers before He reigns; the Gospels show that the very conversation on the mountain was about His departure, Luke 9:31. And He is the beloved Son, given up like Isaac, Genesis 22:2, yet this time the knife falls. Because Peter had heard Jesus speak of the cross just before the mountain, Matthew 16:21 to 23, the glory and the cross are not rivals in his mind. The mountain shows who dies.

The prophets are Christ's witnesses too. Peter says in his first letter that the Spirit of Christ was in them, pointing to 'the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow', 1 Peter 1:11. The prophetic word that is a lamp is a word about Him. Jesus said the same on the road to Emmaus, Luke 24:27, and Hebrews 1:1 and 2 treats the prophets as earlier speech of the same God who now speaks in a Son.

The morning star completes the picture. Numbers 24:17 looks for a star from Jacob, and Revelation 22:16 has Jesus say 'I am the root and offspring of David, and the bright Morning Star'. He is the light the prophets looked for, and in Revelation 2:28 He gives it to those who overcome, so that His people share His dawn. We should be careful not to force every detail. Peter does not say the lamp is Christ; the lamp is the prophetic word, and the star is Christ. The two are linked by direction rather than identified: the word shows the way toward the star and is vindicated when the star appears.
study.god:
The passage shows God as one who speaks. At the mountain the Father speaks to the Son in the hearing of men, and through the prophets He speaks in words that can be read. Peter's whole defence of the gospel depends on a God who communicates, who does not leave human beings to guess about Him. The God of Peter's letter is not a silent first cause but a Father who says, in the hearing of fishermen, who His Son is.

The passage also holds together the Trinity as the speaker. The Father gives honor and glory to the Son, the Spirit carries the prophets, and the Son is the One whose glory is seen. Nothing in the verses explains how three persons are one God, and Peter does not try; he simply lets each act in turn, as the Gospels do at the Jordan.

The God of this passage is also faithful across time. The same Spirit who moved the prophets stands behind the apostles, and the same purposes run from the prophets to the mountain to the letter now being written. That consistency is what makes verse 19 possible: a word spoken long ago is still reliable because the One who spoke it has not changed. Psalm 119 sings the same truth about the lamp.

There is a tension Peter allows to stand. Scripture is fully God's word and fully the word of men, 'men spoke from God'. God does not override the human writers; He carries them. That is a pattern of how God usually works, through chosen persons and ordinary instruments, without ceasing to be the author.

Finally, the passage shows God's kindness in giving light before the dawn. He does not leave His people in the dark until the end; He supplies a lamp. For worship this means that attention to the word is not a duty alongside devotion but the form that devotion takes between now and the Day. We wait for the star, and while we wait we read, because the God who speaks has not stopped being the God who is worth listening to.

crossReferences.note: The same mountain scene told from the inside. Matthew adds that Jesus' face shone like the sun, that Moses and Elijah appeared, and that the Father's voice ends with a command, 'Listen to Him!' Comparing it with Peter's brief account shows how selective and deliberate his version is.

Luke alone says that Moses and Elijah spoke about Jesus' departure, the word Peter takes for his own death in verse 15. The Transfiguration is therefore as much about the cross that lay ahead as about glory.

John's claim of eyewitness, 'We have seen His glory', stands next to Peter's. Both men write as those who saw, and both say the glory was the glory of the Son from the Father, so the testimony of the apostles forms a chain.

Paul says Scripture is God-breathed and useful to equip the believer. Peter names the Spirit's carrying of the writers, Paul names God's breath in the writings; together they describe both the origin and the use of the Bible.

David's last words claim that the Spirit of the LORD spoke through him and that His word was on his tongue. This is the Old Testament form of Peter's claim, and shows he is repeating Israel's settled view of prophecy, not inventing a new one.

Peter explains elsewhere what carried the prophets: the Spirit of Christ in them, pointing to Christ's sufferings and the glories to follow. They searched into their own words, which shows they were not mere secretaries, and that their message was bigger than they knew.

Balaam, of all people, sees a star coming out of Jacob and a scepter rising from Israel. The image of a rising star lies behind the 'morning star' of verse 19, and the way Balaam said it, 'not now' and 'not near', fits the waiting Peter speaks of.
Jesus calls Himself the bright Morning Star. This is the clearest New Testament identification of the star with Himself, and it brings Peter's closing image of the paragraph to the end of the Bible.

God spoke to the fathers through the prophets in many ways and now speaks by His Son. This text gives the same shape as 2 Peter 1: the prophets' word is real and reliable, and it reaches its goal in the Son.

Jesus told Peter what kind of death he would die, and Peter's 'as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me' in verse 14 points back to it. The man now writing the letter has been waiting for this ending since the shore of Galilee.

Peter later counts Paul's letters among 'the Scriptures'. Read beside 1:20 and 21, it shows that for Peter the carrying of the Spirit was still going on while he wrote, and that the apostolic writings stood alongside the prophets.

study.oneStory:
The paragraph answers a question that begins in Genesis 3: how can a fallen human being know the truth about God? The serpent's first move was to question what God had said, Genesis 3:1, and every false story since has begun there. The Bible's answer is that God does not leave His creatures to speculate. He speaks, and He has given that speech a form that can be handed down, first to Adam and Noah, then to Abraham and Moses, and then through the prophets who were carried along by the Spirit.

The long thread of the Old Testament runs toward a day. Israel's prophets look ahead to the star of Jacob, to the Prophet like Moses, to the Servant and the Son of David, and they confess that they do not know the time, 1 Peter 1:11. On the mountain, three men see what the prophets could not: the Servant is the Son, and His glory is the glory of Sinai standing in a human face. Peter's letter then does what Moses did before his death in Deuteronomy, leaving a testimony so that the people will remember and obey after the teacher is gone.

The passage also looks forward to what chapter 2 and chapter 3 will bring. Teachers will arise who bend the word, and scoffers will ask where the promise has gone. Peter's answer is to hold the lamp, to keep the apostolic memory, and to watch for the dawn. The same pattern is in Hebrews 1:1 to 2 and in Jesus' last charge in Acts 1:8, where the apostles are made witnesses to the ends of the earth.

The morning star links this paragraph to the end of the story. The Star who is Jesus comes at the last, and Revelation 22:5 says there will be no night and no need of lamp or sun because the Lord God will give them light. The lamp is for the long night between the mountain and the dawn; when the dawn comes, the lamp is not discarded but fulfilled, because what it pointed to has arrived and the word has been proved true. In the new creation, those who believed on the strength of a Voice and a written word will see the One whose glory Peter glimpsed on a mountain, and Peter's own exodos will have led where Jesus' led, into the presence of the Father.

sermon.title: An Eyewitness Account
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in 2 Peter, this message treats 2 Peter 1:12-21 directly, Peter's farewell reminder, the eyewitness testimony of the Transfiguration, and the divine origin of the prophetic word. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement.

quiz.q: Why does Peter keep reminding the church of these truths?

options.text: Because he knows he will die soon and wants them to remember after his departure.
options.note: Verses 13 to 15: he writes as a farewell, so the truths will endure past his death.

options.text: Because he doubts whether the truths are actually reliable.
options.note: The opposite: he is utterly confident, grounding the truths in eyewitness and Scripture.

options.text: Because the readers had never heard these things before.
options.note: They already know them and are established; he reminds rather than introduces.

options.text: Because he wants them established and unshaken in the truth.
options.note: True and part of his aim, though the stated reason is his approaching death.

quiz.q: What does Peter appeal to as proof that the gospel is not a myth?

options.text: He was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty and heard God's voice at the Transfiguration.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18: firsthand sight and the Father's voice, not invented tales.

options.text: The cleverness of the arguments the apostles devised.
options.note: He explicitly denies following cleverly devised fables.

options.text: That he was present with Jesus on the holy mountain.
options.note: True, that is the setting, though the point is his eyewitness of Christ's majesty.

options.text: The wide popularity of the Christian message.
options.note: Peter grounds truth in witnessed events, not popularity.

quiz.q: According to verses 20 to 21, where did the prophetic Scriptures come from?

options.text: From God, as men spoke while carried along by the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verse 21: not the will of man, but the Spirit moving the prophets.

options.text: From the prophets' own insight and imagination.
options.note: Peter expressly denies that prophecy came by the will of man.

options.text: From men moved by the Spirit while still writing as real authors.
options.note: True to the doctrine of inspiration, both divine and human, though it should name God as the source.

options.text: From the collected wisdom of Israel's traditions.
options.note: The source is the Holy Spirit, not merely human tradition.

quiz.q: How does Peter rank the prophetic word alongside his own eyewitness experience?

options.text: The written prophetic word is fully confirmed and to be heeded as a lamp until Christ dawns.
options.note: Verse 19: Scripture is the sure lamp; experience is tested by the word, not above it.

options.text: Personal experience always outranks the written word.
options.note: Peter points to the prophetic word as even more sure than his vision.

options.text: The two agree, both testifying to Christ.
options.note: True, they agree, though Peter's stress falls on the reliability of the written word.

options.text: The prophetic word is useful only until we have our own experiences.
options.note: The lamp shines until Christ Himself appears, not until private experience replaces it.

quiz.q: What is the morning star Peter longs to see rise in his readers' hearts?

options.text: Christ Himself, whose full appearing ends the night the prophetic lamp guides us through.
options.note: Verse 19 points to Christ, the bright morning star of Revelation 22:16.

options.text: A literal star that will appear in the sky.
options.note: The image is of Christ's dawning, not a mere astronomical event.

options.text: The dawning light of Christ growing bright within believers.
options.note: True to the image, though it is finally Christ Himself who rises.

options.text: The believer's own inner enlightenment apart from Christ.
options.note: The light is Christ, not a self-generated illumination.

questions: Peter calls his coming death a departure and his body a tent. How does viewing the body as a temporary dwelling change the way you face aging, illness, or death?
The gospel rests on eyewitness testimony, not clever myths. How does the historical, witnessed nature of the faith strengthen your confidence in it?
Peter treats the written Scriptures as even more sure than his own vision of glory. Where are you tempted to trust your experiences over God's word, and how might you reverse that?
The prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit. How does believing that the Bible is truly God's word shape the way you read and obey it?
Peter longs for the morning star to rise in his readers' hearts. What would it look like for you to live today in eager hope of Christ's appearing?

translationNotes.note: The tent of my body renders skenoma; a footnote notes the literal as long as I am in this tent, picturing the body as a temporary dwelling.
Departure translates exodos, the same word used of Jesus' death at the Transfiguration in Luke 9:31.
The Father's words echo Matthew 17:5; see also Mark 9:7 and Luke 9:35, the voice at the Transfiguration.
One's own interpretation renders epilysis; in context, clarified by verse 21, it concerns the divine origin of prophecy rather than private reading, though it also guards against twisting the text.
